title: Vowels — あ い う え お

points.name: あ
points.explanation: The vowel あ is the very first character in the hiragana syllabary, and it's one of the most satisfying sounds to get right immediately. Pronounce it like the 'a' in 'father' or 'spa' — a wide-open, relaxed sound produced at the back of the mouth. Unlike English, where the letter 'a' has a dozen different pronunciations (think 'cat', 'cake', 'care', 'sofa'), Japanese あ never changes: it sounds exactly the same in every single word, every time. This consistency is one of the great joys of Japanese — once you learn the five vowels, you can sound out virtually any hiragana word and be understood. あ kicks off the vowel row that anchors the entire kana chart.
rules: Open your mouth wide and relax your jaw — think of saying 'ah' at the doctor's office.
Don't tense or round your lips; this is a pure, open vowel with no glide into another sound.
Length matters: short あ is one beat, but ああ (written doubled) is two beats — always keep it crisp unless you see it doubled.

points.name: い
points.explanation: The vowel い produces a bright, forward 'ee' sound, exactly like the vowel in 'feet' or 'see'. To hit it correctly, spread your lips slightly as if you're beginning a small smile — your tongue rises naturally toward the front of the roof of your mouth. Japanese speakers keep い short and pure, without the slight 'y' glide that English speakers often add unconsciously (English 'see' actually ends with a tiny 'y' sound; Japanese い does not). You will encounter い constantly in Japanese: it ends most adjectives, appears in grammatical structures everywhere, and is one of the most frequent sounds in the entire language.
rules: Smile gently — this positions your lips and tongue correctly for the bright 'ee' quality.
Stop cleanly at the end; resist adding any 'y' glide after the vowel.
In fast speech い can become nearly silent between certain consonants, but focus on its full 'ee' sound for now.

points.name: う
points.shortDescription: Like 'oo' in 'food' but with relaxed, flat lips
points.explanation: The vowel う is the trickiest of the five Japanese vowels for English speakers because it doesn't match any English vowel exactly. It's similar to the 'oo' in 'food', but the critical difference is that your lips should be relaxed and nearly flat — not rounded and pushed forward as in English 'oo'. Think of what your mouth does when you say 'hmm' in a neutral tone, then raise the back of your tongue slightly. Some teachers describe it as a 'dull oo' or 'compressed oo'. This unrounded quality is distinctive to Japanese (and a few other East Asian languages) and will take a bit of practice to produce naturally.
rules: Do NOT round or push out your lips — this is the single biggest difference from English 'oo'.
Keep your lips relaxed and nearly flat while the back of your tongue rises.
う is short by default; only lengthen it when you see うう or a long-vowel marker.
points.flashcardAnswer: u — like 'oo' in 'food' but with relaxed, flat lips

points.name: え
points.explanation: The vowel え sounds like the 'e' in 'bed' or 'set' — a clean mid-front vowel that English speakers can nail right away. Your mouth opens to a medium width, and your tongue sits at a middle height in your mouth, neither too high nor too low. Unlike the English 'ay' in 'late' (which glides into a 'y' sound), Japanese え is pure and stationary — the sound starts and stops cleanly with no movement. You will encounter え frequently in Japanese grammar and everyday vocabulary, including as part of the direction particle meaning 'toward'.
rules: Medium mouth opening — wider than い but not as wide as あ.
Keep it pure: no 'y' glide or movement at the end, unlike the English 'ay' in 'say'.
Think 'eh' rather than 'ay' — flat and brief, like a short version of the 'e' in 'bed'.

points.name: お
points.explanation: The vowel お produces a round, mid-back 'oh' sound, close to the 'o' in 'open' or 'go' — but without the glide that English speakers naturally add. In English, 'go' actually sounds more like 'goh-w', ending with a hint of 'w' as the lips round further. Japanese お stops cleanly without that movement. Round your lips moderately and let the sound ring steady. You will hear お constantly in Japanese, including in the honorific prefix お- that makes everyday words polite — so mastering this vowel is immediately useful.
rules: Round your lips moderately, but don't push them far forward into an 'oo' shape.
Stop cleanly without your lips spreading or moving toward a 'w' sound at the end.
Watch for long vowels: both おお and おう indicate a lengthened 'o' sound, spoken as two beats.

chapterPractice.prompt: What sound does this character make?
chapterPractice.explanation: あ makes the 'a' sound, like the 'a' in 'father'. It's the first vowel in Japanese and has a wide-open, pure sound.

chapterPractice.prompt: Which character makes the 'e' sound (like the 'e' in 'bed')?
chapterPractice.explanation: え makes the 'e' sound, like the 'e' in 'bed'. It's a clean mid-front vowel with no glide.
あい (ai) means 'love' in Japanese. You can hear both vowels clearly: あ (a) + い (i).
うえ (ue) means 'above' or 'up'. It combines う (u) + え (e) — two of the five Japanese vowels.
